claims.claim: ⚠️ **These children may deteriorate rapidly or become extremely agitated, aggressive and violent**, and may conceal or deny use because of how parents may respond.
claims.source_text: The assessment and management of children presenting with acute intoxication, withdrawal or toxicity can be demanding and potentially dangerous. These children may rapidly deteriorate or may become extremely agitated, aggressive and violent. Young people may conceal or deny substance use because of potential parent/guardian responses.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Response to a drug depends on** the individual (age, size, gender, health, mood), the drug's pharmacology and pharmacokinetics, the dose, the setting, combinations with other substances, and previous experience.
claims.source_text: characteristics of the individual (eg age, size, gender, health state, mood etc.) pharmacology of the drug/s used pharmacokinetics of drug/s used dosage of the drug/s taken … the setting in which the drug/s were used drug/s used in combination with other substances (inc. medicines, inhalants, herbal preparations) previous experience with the drug/s used
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Even small or infrequent use can cause a dramatic response** in a young person with underlying psychological or psychiatric issues.
claims.source_text: Small or infrequent use of any substance in a young person with underlying psychological or psychiatric issues may cause a dramatic and significant response.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intoxication signs:** slurred speech, poor concentration, altered perception, agitation, confusion, disorientation, unstable mood or gait, vomiting, diarrhoea, incontinence.
claims.source_text: Common symptoms and signs of intoxication include: Slurred speech Poor concentration Altered perception Agitation Confusion Disorientation Unstable mood Unstable gait Vomiting, diarrhoea, incontinence
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Exclude medical causes first:** head injury, acute infection, electrolyte imbalance, CVA, hypoglycaemia, psychosis, severe liver disease.
claims.source_text: Exclude possible medical or biological reasons for the presentation (eg head injury, acute infection, electrolyte imbalance, CVA, hypoglycemia, psychosis, severe liver disease etc.)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Take an alcohol and other drug (AOD) history** — what, when and how much today; if the child cannot or will not say, **use collateral sources** (companions, parents, family, guardians).
claims.source_text: Take an Alcohol and other Drug (AOD) use history. Enquire about AOD use on the day of presentation and the time and quantity of recently consumed substances. If the child is unwilling or unable to provide an AOD use history, attempt to identify collateral sources for obtaining information i.e. companions, parents, family, guardians etc.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine for signs of use:** puncture marks, cellulitis, phlebitis, abscesses, nasal erosion, irritation or rash around nostrils or mouth, rectal damage, dehydration, rapid weight loss.
claims.source_text: Examine for physical signs of drug use such as puncture marks, cellulitis, phlebitis, skin abscesses, nasal erosion, irritation or rash around nostrils, septum or mouth, evidence of rectal damage, dehydration, rapid weight loss.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review general functioning and psychosocial circumstances; consult mental health** if background mental health issues are suspected.
claims.source_text: Review the child's general functioning and psychosocial circumstances. Consult with the mental health service if background mental health issues are suspected.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A simple, quiet, uncluttered room; as few staff as possible; a calm, confident, respectful approach**; speak clearly and slowly and use the child's name.
claims.source_text: Create a simple, quiet, and uncluttered environment - remove unnecessary equipment Minimise the number of staff attending the child Treat the child with respect Approach in a quiet, calm and confident manner Speak clearly and slowly Use the child's proper name when speaking to them
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Brief, frequent reassurance** helps avoid agitation. ⚠️ **Protect from accidental harm** — never leave them on a bed without safety guards; lower the bed as close to the floor as possible.
claims.source_text: Provide frequent reassurance. Brief and frequent attendances will assist with this and may avoid unnecessary agitation Protect the child from accidental harm (eg do not leave them unattended on a bed without safety guards. Lower the bed as close to the floor as possible)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For the confused child:** regular reality orientation, a familiar object in view, correct perceptual errors, accompany them to the toilet.
claims.source_text: Provide regular reality orientation For the confused/disoriented child, keep an object familiar to them in view (eg a bag or an item of clothing) Correct perceptual errors and tell the child what is real … Accompany the person to and from places (eg toilet)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Aggressive child:** keep space and an easy exit, don't crowd them, keep furniture between you, **work in pairs or call security** if at risk; try to identify and remove the cause of anger.
claims.source_text: In the case of aggressive children- use space for self-protection (eg ensure you have easy access to the open door, do not 'crowd' them, keep furniture between yourself and the person, etc). Work in pairs or request security if you feel at risk Be flexible when dealing an aggressive child- try to identify the cause of their anger and if possible, remove it
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A child refusing treatment and wanting to leave when unsafe:** you may need to exercise your duty of care — follow Code response procedures and consult senior staff.
claims.source_text: If a chid is refusing treatment and wishes to leave the hospital when it is unsafe to do so, you may need to exercise your duty of care to ensure their safety and wellbeing. Refer to Code response procedures. Consult senior staff.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Observe and monitor intoxicated or withdrawing children closely** — they are at risk of medical complications.
claims.source_text: Children presenting as intoxicated or in withdrawal should be observed and monitored closely as they are at risk of medical complication
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Alcohol withdrawal can start before the blood alcohol reading reaches zero.** Seizures may signal alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, or stimulant intoxication.
claims.source_text: Note that alcohol withdrawal can occur before a zero blood alcohol reading Seizures may be an indication of alcohol withdrawal, benzodiazepine withdrawal or stimulant intoxication.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Once an intoxicated child seems stable, reassess for withdrawal** — early recognition and treatment can prevent life-threatening complications.
claims.source_text: Children who appear to have stabilised after being intoxicated should be further assessed for any possibility of withdrawal - early identification and treatment for withdrawal can prevent potentially life-threatening complications.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer to the child's primary health practitioner**, and consider a specialist AOD or mental health service. **If AOD raises concern for future care or safety, consider notifying Child Protective Services.**
claims.source_text: Following assessment and acute management of the intoxicated presentation, a referral to the child's primary health practitioner should be made. In appropriate circumstances a referral to a specialist AOD or mental health service should be considered. … If there are concerns about the young person's future care or safety due to AOD, consider notification to Child Protective Services
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Substance use (abuse)' (undated page), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Substance_use_abuse/, retrieved 2026-09-23
